nameStory: The name 'sandbur' perfectly captures this grass's dual nature - it thrives in sandy coastal areas and produces wickedly spiny burs that grab onto anything passing by. The 'coastal' part of its common name reflects its preference for shoreline habitats, where it's often the first plant brave enough to colonize loose, shifting sands.
description: Coastal sandbur is a tough, low-growing perennial grass that forms clumps in sandy areas along New England's coast. Growing 5 to 30 inches tall, it has narrow grass blades and produces the infamous spiny seed heads (called burs) that make it memorable to anyone who's stepped on one barefoot. This southern native has crept northward and established small populations in our region, where it's considered quite rare.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The unmistakable spiny burs contain 8-40 sharp, backward-pointing barbs that feel like tiny fishhooks and stick painfully to skin, socks, and pet fur - once you've encountered them, you'll never forget this plant

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading clumps that hug the ground, with stems that often sprawl outward before turning upright, creating patches rather than single upright stalks

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, flat grass blades that feel rough to the touch and have a blue-green color, growing alternately along the stems in typical grass fashion

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous grass flowers appear in dense, cylindrical clusters before developing into the notorious spiny burs

habitat: In New England, look for coastal sandbur in sandy coastal areas, dunes, and disturbed sandy soils near the shore. It thrives in the loose, well-drained sandy or gravelly terrain that many other plants can't tolerate. Given its extreme rarity here with only one recorded observation, it's more of a botanical curiosity than a common coastal resident.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with fresh green shoots appearing from overwintering crowns.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their small grass flowers, which quickly develop into the spiny seed heads.
seasonality.fall: The mature burs are at their stickiest and most painful, ready to hitch rides on passing animals and humans to new locations.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts may die back in harsh New England winters, but the perennial roots survive to regrow next spring.

funFact: Each spiny bur is essentially a medieval mace in miniature - the backward-pointing barbs are so effective that they inspired the design of modern Velcro, and a single plant can produce hundreds of these natural hitchhikers in a season.
confusionNotes: The spiny burs make this nearly impossible to confuse with anything else once they're present - no other New England grass produces such painful, sticky seed heads. Before the burs form, it might blend in with other coastal grasses, but the low, sprawling growth habit in sandy areas is a good clue.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common sandbur' in some regions, this grass is actually extremely rare in New England - a reminder that common names can be misleading depending on where you are. What's common in Texas or Florida might be a botanical treasure in Massachusetts.
compareHints: Coastal sandbur differs from its relative mat sandbur by preferring coastal sandy habitats rather than inland disturbed areas. Chinese pennisetum, another Cenchrus relative, produces showy, bottle-brush-like flower heads that are ornamental rather than painfully spiny. The sprawling, clumping growth habit also sets coastal sandbur apart from the more upright fountain grass relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mat sandbur differs from its coastal relative, coastal sandbur, by its lower, more spreading growth habit and slightly smaller burs.

Unlike its Cenchrus relatives mat sandbur and coastal sandbur, which are low-growing weedy grasses with spiny, painful seed burs, Chinese pennisetum is a tall, ornamental clumping grass with soft, feathery plumes.
